A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same REPARO work, with matching authors, core methodology and experiments. All supplied pages were inspected, including v1 Appendix A. v2 ends with references and contains no appendix, although it mentions supplementary user-study material.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original reconstruction experiments, quantitative comparisons, loss ablations, qualitative results and a 40-participant user study.

after.justification: Section 4 reports reconstruction and user-study results, together with additional parameter ablations, ground-truth-asset controls, resource measurements and editing demonstrations.

M1.justification: The two-stage pipeline and loss functions remain. Section 3.2 changes layout optimization from translation and rotation to translation and per-axis scale, explicitly fixing rotation; Section 4.4 adds an AnyDoor-based editing extension. These are limited procedural changes, although v2 Section 4.1 inconsistently retains the translation-and-rotation description.

E1.justification: The GSO reconstruction evaluation and additional qualitative-image coverage remain. v2 Section 4.4 and Figure 7 extend the evaluated task to 2D-guided 3D scene editing, demonstrating object addition, removal, position exchange and instance replacement. This substantially broadens task requirements beyond reconstruction from an unchanged image.

E2.justification: v2 adds standalone TripoSR to the quantitative comparison in Table 1 and qualitative comparison in Figure 4. v1 used TripoSR within REPARO but did not evaluate it as a standalone comparator there. DreamGaussian, Wonder3D and LRM remain.

E3.justification: The 20-scene GSO evaluation, 18 evaluation views, four image metrics, 40 participants and 500-iteration budget remain. v2 adds controlled translation/rotation/scale configurations, a ground-truth-asset control and runtime/VRAM comparisons. The reported final parameter configuration changes, although the implementation paragraph is inconsistent; omitted hyperparameters do not establish additional setting changes.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of which scene parameters to optimize (Table 5 and Figures 3 and 5) and how first-stage asset quality affects results (Table 7), plus editing case studies. The existing loss ablations remain, but v1 Appendix A's qualitative local-loss-versus-OT comparison is absent from the supplied v2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or significance tests. The user-study preference percentages retain the same aggregation practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds standalone TripoSR, parameter-control, ground-truth-asset, resource and editing results. Existing REPARO values also change: Table 1 PSNR changes from 17.391 to 17.279 for DreamGaussian-based REPARO and from 17.778 to 17.751 for TripoSR-based REPARO, with corresponding ablation updates. The revised optimization description prevents treating these as established same-setting performance changes. Existing baseline scores and user-study preference percentages remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 3 repairs the malformed demand-side mass-conservation sum, replacing the incorrectly indexed sum in v1 with the sum of d_j from j=1 to M. The remaining mathematics is substantively retained; Equation 5 merely abbreviates the existing appearance loss using the previously defined transport cost.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: compositional reconstruction through separate object generation and layout alignment, an OT-based RGB/depth/position loss, and semantic-feature alignment improving scene coherence. The contribution list is rewritten without materially redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises the explanations and limitations. It motivates fixing rotation through preservation of input orientation, attributes errors to first-stage asset generation, and identifies hallucinations under severe occlusion and common-sense bias in implausible scenes. It removes v1's discussion of disagreement between quantitative metrics and visual layout quality, including the appendix explanation supporting that concern.

D1.justification: v2 omits v1's 256-by-256 resolution, specific depth/feature model variants, GeomLoss implementation and epsilon=0.01, lambda=0.9, and 200-iteration semantic-loss warm-up. It also omits the 280-response count and user-study randomization/time-constraint details. Conversely, it adds per-stage runtime/VRAM information, identifies AnyDoor for editing and changes the listed demo address. These substantially change reproducibility documentation without establishing that omitted settings changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to AnyDoor, LangSplat, 4D LangSplat and Mip-Splatting, while removing works including DMV3D and Disentangled 3D Scene Generation with Layout Learning. It drops the transformer/triplane reconstruction paragraph and condenses compositional related work. The overall positioning as single-image compositional generation remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are extensively rewritten and reordered, and related work is substantially condensed. Experimental reporting is reorganized, the user study is shortened, and an editing subsection is introduced. These are substantial narrative changes, although much of the method exposition remains.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the pipeline diagram, expands the opening comparison with geometry views, and replaces the compact qualitative comparison with a full-page multiview matrix. It adds resource/control tables and parameter/editing figures. The standalone asset gallery, user-study pie chart and appendix comparison disappear, while the appearance-loss visualization is retained at a smaller size.

improvement.justification: The added TripoSR comparison, parameter and ground-truth controls, resource accounting and concrete limitations provide useful evidence. However, v2 removes essential reproducibility settings and appendix evidence, retains conflicting descriptions of optimized variables, and incorrectly calls translation-plus-scale the lowest-LPIPS DreamGaussian setting: Table 5 gives 0.234 versus 0.232 for translation alone. These losses in reproducibility and internal consistency counter the empirical gains, preventing a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
